issues.legal_issue: A claim to recover earnest money paid as security for performance, where the transaction was never completed, is governed by the residuary limitation rule when no specific limitation category covers the claim.
material_facts: A buyer paid an amount as earnest money to evidence bona fides and secure performance of an agreement to sell.
The transaction did not proceed to completion, and later legal restrictions made the agreed transfer unlawful.
The buyer sought restoration of the earnest money.
issues.conclusion: The claim for the earnest money was governed by the residuary Article 120 and was within time.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 65 of the Contract Act, a person who has received an advantage under an agreement that becomes void must restore it or compensate the person from whom it was received. Article 97 applies to money paid upon an existing consideration that later fails, while Article 62 concerns money received for the plaintiff’s use; neither covered this earnest money because it was paid as collateral security and would become part of the purchase price only if the transaction proceeded. Article 120 applies where no other limitation article covers the claim. Limitation provisions are construed strictly and should not be stretched to bar a claim unless their plain language clearly does so. The court distinguished Ram Labhaya v. Municipal Committee, Amritsar, Rayangonda Anna Patil v. Jankibai, Udit Narain Misra v. Muhammad Minnat Ullal, and other cited decisions because they did not decide the limitation treatment of earnest money in comparable circumstances.

rule.if: refund_claim_in_contract_dispute and earnest_money_paid_as_security and transaction_not_completed and not earnest_money_paid_as_purchase_price

predicates.refund_claim_in_contract_dispute: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid in connection with an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.earnest_money_paid_as_security: The payer gave the money as security for performance and evidence of bona fides.
predicates.transaction_not_completed: The agreed transfer did not proceed to completion.
predicates.earnest_money_paid_as_purchase_price: The money was paid as part of the purchase price rather than as security.

issues.definition: When a repayment claim concerns an uncompleted transaction and the money was security rather than purchase-price payment, the claim is timely under the residuary limitation rule.

issues.legal_issue: An advance paid toward the purchase price, unlike earnest money paid as security, is governed by the limitation rule for money paid upon consideration that later fails.
material_facts: The buyer paid an additional advance toward the purchase price, rather than as earnest money or collateral security.
The agreed transfer became unlawful under evacuee-property legislation before the buyer filed the claim.
The claim for repayment of the additional advance was filed after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.
issues.conclusion: The additional advance was governed by Article 97, and the claim for its repayment was time-barred.
issues.legal_principle: Article 97 applies to money paid upon an existing consideration that afterwards fails. The court distinguished such a payment toward the purchase price from earnest money, which serves as security and becomes part of the price only if the transaction proceeds. The court also relied on the distinction between repayment of a purchase-price payment and recovery of earnest money when applying the limitation provisions.

rule.if: refund_claim_in_contract_dispute and advance_paid_toward_purchase_price and consideration_later_failed and claim_filed_after_limitation_period_elapsed

predicates.refund_claim_in_contract_dispute: A claimant seeks repayment of money paid in connection with an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.advance_paid_toward_purchase_price: The payer gave the money as an advance toward the purchase price rather than as security.
predicates.consideration_later_failed: The transfer for which the payment was made later became incapable of performance.
predicates.claim_filed_after_limitation_period_elap: The claimant filed the repayment claim after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.

issues.definition: A repayment claim is time-barred when an advance toward the purchase price was paid for a transfer that later became incapable of performance and the claim was filed after the applicable limitation period.

issues.legal_issue: An extension of limitation for a debt-adjustment proceeding does not save a claim when the agreed transfer had already become unlawful before the claim was filed.
material_facts: The buyer pursued a debt claim through a statutory debt-adjustment proceeding.
Legislation governing evacuee property prohibited the agreed transfer before the buyer filed the proceeding.
The buyer argued that the statutory extension of limitation saved the claim.
issues.conclusion: The statutory extension did not save the claim for the purchase-price advance because the prohibition on the transfer had taken effect before the claim was filed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(a) of the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act was invoked as extending limitation for proceedings under that Act. The court held that the extension could not save the claim on the asserted basis because the legislation making performance of the sale unlawful had come into force before the application was filed.

predicates.debt_adjustment_proceeding: The claimant seeks recovery through a statutory proceeding for adjustment of debts.
predicates.transfer_prohibited_before_claim_filed: A legal prohibition on the agreed transfer took effect before the claimant filed the proceeding.

issues.definition: In a debt-adjustment proceeding, a limitation extension does not save a claim when the agreed transfer was prohibited before the proceeding was filed.
